en: Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. (1.1.1) [Brahman is that] from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]. (1.1.2) Because it has the scripture as its source. (1.1.3)

But that [Brahman is the cause] because of the harmony [of the texts]; (1.1.4) because of the act of seeing, it is not that which is not based on scripture; (1.1.5) if it be argued that [the term "Self"] is secondary, we say no, because of the word "Self. (1.1.6)
Because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to that; because there is no statement regarding its being something to be abandoned;
and because it would contradict the initial proposition.
Because of [the Lord's] going to sleep;
because of the uniformity of the mode of transition;
and because it is so stated in scripture.
"The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition;
if it be argued that it is not so because of the word denoting a modification, we say no, because of abundance;
and also because of the designation of its cause."
And it is described as being based precisely on the wording of the mantra;
not the other [the individual soul], because that is untenable;
and because there is a designation of difference.
And because of desire, there is no dependence on inference (BBs 1.1.19).
It teaches his connection with this [body] while he is in it (BBs 1.1.20),
because of the instruction regarding those qualities within [the body] (BBs 1.1.21).
And [the Self] is other [than the body] because of the designation of difference (BBs 1.1.22). Space [is other than the body] because of its characteristic mark (BBs 1.1.23).
For this very reason, the vital breath [is other than the body] (BBs 1.1.24).

Because of the mention of "feet" in the word *jyotis*. (BBs 1.1.25) If it is argued that it is not so because of the mention of a *chandas* (meter), we say no; for there is a declaration of the fixing of the mind [on Brahman] in that manner, and there is a scriptural vision to that effect. (BBs 1.1.26) And because the designation of the "feet" as the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth is thus appropriate. (BBs 1.1.27)
If it be argued that [the breath] is not [the Self] because of the difference in instruction, we say no, for there is no contradiction in either case.
(BBs 1.1.28) The breath [is the Self] because it is so understood [in other passages].

(BBs 1.1.29) If it be argued that it is not so because of the instruction regarding the Self of the speaker, [we reply that] this is not the case, for in this [passage] there is an abundance of references to the internal [Self]. (BBs 1.1.30)
But the instruction is according to the perspective of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva.

(BBs 1.1.31) If it be argued that it is not so because of the characteristic marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*prāṇa*), we say no; because of the threefold nature of meditation, because [the soul] is dependent [on the body], and because of its connection with that [state] here.
(BBs 1.1.32) Because of the instruction regarding what is well-known everywhere. (BBs 1.2.1)
And because the intended qualities are possible [in that case];
but because they are not possible [in the other], it is not the embodied soul;
and because of the designation of the object and the agent [of action].
Because of the distinction of the word;
and because of memory.
If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the agent] because of its smallness and because of that designation, we say no, precisely because it is to be perceived as such, and because it is like space.
If it be argued that [the Self] is the attainment of enjoyment, we say no, because of its distinctness;
because the Self is the grasper of both the moving and the unmoving;
and because of the context.
For the two selves have entered the cave, because that is seen [in scripture];
and because of the qualification;
and because of the appropriateness of the inner [self].
And because of the designation of its abode and so forth;
and because of the mention of its distinction from pleasure;
for this very reason, it is Brahman.
And because of the description of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads;
and because of non-abiding and impossibility, it is not the other.
[The Lord is] the Inner Controller with respect to the deities, the worlds, and so forth, because of the designation of His attributes.

Nor is it the one mentioned in the Smṛti, because its attributes are not described there; nor is it the embodied soul, for both [recensions] study this [Self] as distinct [from them]. It is the one characterized by invisibility and other qualities, because of the mention of its attributes.
And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, it is neither of the other two;
also because of the presentation of form.
Vaiśvānara [is the Self] because of the specific [use of] common terms.
"It might be argued that what is being remembered is [simply] inference;

[but this is not so], because of the mention of sound and so forth, and because of its abiding within. If it is objected that it is not so because of the teaching of a vision [of the Self] and because of impossibility, [we reply: no, for they also study this as the Puruṣa.
For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being. (BBs 1.2.26–28)
Jaimini [holds that] there is no contradiction even with direct perception;
Āśmarathya [says it is so] because of manifestation;
Bādari [says it is so] because of recollection.
"Jaimini [holds that it refers to the state of] attainment, for scripture shows it so;
and they record him in this [state];
the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word. (BS 1.2.32–34)
And because there is a designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated;
and it is not inference, because the word for it is not such, and because of the vital breath;
and because of the designation of difference.
Because of the context;
because of abiding and eating;
and because of the instruction concerning the abundance [of bliss] beyond the serene faith.
And because of the occurrence of the term *dharma*;
and [the Imperishable is Brahman] because it supports everything up to the sky;
and that [supporting] is due to its command.
And because of the exclusion of other states;
"He is [Brahman] because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing"; "The small one [is Brahman] because of the subsequent [arguments]."
For it is seen from the words "going" and "sound," as well as from the mark;
and because of its support, and because of its greatness being perceived in this [world],
and because of its renown.
If it is argued that "He" [refers to the individual soul] because of the subsequent reference, we say no, because of impossibility (BBs 1.3.17).
If it is argued that it refers to him because of the later statement, [we reply] that his true nature has indeed become manifest (BBs 1.3.18).
Furthermore, the reference is for another purpose (BBs 1.3.19).
If it is argued that [the individual soul] is meant because of its limited hearing, that has already been answered. Furthermore, on account of its imitation of Him,
and moreover, it is so recorded in Smṛti.
[The qualification for knowledge] is established by scripture alone;
however, with respect to the heart, it concerns human beings because [the scriptures] have humans as their primary audience. Bādarāyaṇa holds that it extends even above them, because it is possible.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe multiple forms of realization.
If it is argued that this refers to sound, we say no, because [the world] originates from That, as established by both perception and inference.
And for this very reason, [That] is eternal.
And because name and form are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of returning, as is seen from scripture and from tradition.

(BBs 1.3.29) Jaimini [holds that] there is no qualification for the gods, because of the impossibility [of it] in the cases of the honey[-meditation] and so forth, and because of their existence in the light [of the sun]. (BBs 1.3.30–31)
But Bādarāyaṇa holds that there is [the qualification of being a Śūdra],
for it is indicated by the hearing of the Śūdra's distress and his subsequent approach;
and because his status as a Kṣatriya is established.
And because of the indicative mark [found] later with regard to Caitraratha;
because of the reference to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*); because of the statement regarding their absence;
and because of the engagement in determining that absence.
Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda];
because of tradition;
and because of trembling.
Because of the perception of light;
because of the designation of space as being a different entity and so forth;
and because of the distinction [of the Self] in deep sleep and at the time of departure.
[The Self is] from words such as "husband" and so forth.

If it be argued that for some [it is] even inferential (ānumānika), we say no; because [the text] shows that [the Self] is grasped as presented through the metaphor of the body, and because it further demonstrates this.
But it is subtle, because it is worthy of that [subtlety].
Because it is dependent on that [the mind], it is meaningful;
and because there is no statement that it is an object of knowledge.
If it is argued that [the scripture] says so, we say no, for the wise [author] did not mean it according to the context.
And there is both the presentation and the question regarding these three alone;
[the term] "the Great" [is used];
and because there is no distinction, it is like the cups.
"But [the soul] has light as its starting point, for thus it is studied by some;
and because of the instruction of a mental construction, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth.
"Nor [is the objection valid] even from the inclusion of the number, because of the absence of knowledge [of the individual souls] and because of the excess [of the number]."
The vital breath and so forth [are the subject] because of the supplementary statements;
for some [texts], light [is the subject] when food is absent;
and [Brahman is the subject] because it is spoken of as the cause in the case of ether and the rest, exactly as it was previously designated.
Because of the drawing together;
because it denotes the world;
if it be argued that [the passage does not refer to Brahman] on account of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), that has already been explained.
Jaimini [holds that the passage] has another meaning, on account of both the question and the explanation; and thus some [teachers] also [hold].
[The passage refers to Brahman] because of the syntactical connection of the sentences.
Āśmarathya [maintains that it is a] sign for the establishment of the initial proposition.
"Audulomi [maintains that the soul departs] from its state as it is about to transmigrate;
Kāśakṛtsna [maintains that it does not depart] because of its persistence [in the body];
and [the soul is] the material cause [of the world], because this avoids contradicting the initial proposition and the illustrative examples."
And because of the teaching of covetousness;
and because both are directly recorded [in scripture];
and because of the creation of the self.
Because of transformation;
for it is indeed proclaimed as the source.
By this, all [points] are explained—truly explained.

If it is argued that this leads to the fault of leaving no room for memory (*smṛti*), we say no; for that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other memories. Furthermore, because others [of such memories] are not perceived, by this the [Yoga] system is refuted.
"It is not so, because this [body] has different characteristics; and its being such [as the Self] is due to the word [of scripture].
(BBs 2.1.4) "But there is a designation based on the one who possesses [the body], because of distinction and because of following [the body].
(BBs 2.1.5) "But it is seen [in the world]. (BBs 2.1.6)
If it be argued that [the world] is non-existent, we say no, because that would be a mere negation.
(BBs 2.1.7) [The doctrine of Brahman as the cause is] inconsistent because, at the time of reabsorption, the same undesirable consequence would apply.
(BBs 2.1.8) But this is not so, because of the existence of illustrative examples. (BBs 2.1.9)
And because of the faults in one's own position;
and also because of the instability of reasoning (*tarka-apratiṣṭhāna*).
If it is argued that the object of inference is otherwise, even so, there follows the consequence of no liberation.
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained.
(2.1.13) If it be argued that there is no distinction because of the attainment of the state of the enjoyer, as in the case of the world;
(2.1.14) The non-difference of that [effect] from Brahman is established on account of the words concerning "origin" and so forth. (2.1.15)
And because [the effect] is perceived when the cause exists;
and because there is another [effect] that exists;

if it is argued that [the cause does not exist] because of the designation of non-existence, we say no, because of the statement of another property in the remainder of the sentence and because of another word.
And like a cloth;
and as in the case of the vital breath and so forth.
Because of the designation of [the Self] as other [than the body], there follows the contingency of defects such as not performing what is beneficial.
But [the objection that the Self is not manifold] is refuted because of the teaching of its differentiation (BBs 2.1.22);
and because it is like a stone and other such things, that [manifoldness] is untenable (BBs 2.1.23).
If it is argued that it is not so because we observe the withdrawal [of the world into Brahman], we say no, for it is like milk (BBs 2.1.24).
Also because, as in the case of gods and others, [the world] exists in the world;
BBs_2,1.25 / [Otherwise, there would be] the consequence of the whole [Brahman] being affected, or else the contradiction of the scriptural statement regarding its partlessness;
BBs_2,1.26 / But on account of scripture, for [Brahman] has the Word as its source. BBs_2,1.27 /
And likewise with respect to the self; for [the world] is indeed manifold;
and because of the faults in one's own position;
and because it is endowed with all [qualities], as seen from that.
If it is argued that [the Lord does not create] because He is devoid of organs, that has already been answered.
(BBs 2.1.31) It is not so, because [creation] serves a purpose. (BBs 2.1.32) But, as in the world, it is mere sport. (BBs 2.1.33)
"Unequal distribution and cruelty [cannot be attributed to the Lord] because He has regard [for karma]; for thus He shows.
If it is argued that [karma] does not exist because there was no prior division [of beings], we say no, because [the cycle] is beginningless; this is both logically established and observed.
And because all dharmas are possible [only on this basis]."
And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [of a creator]; and because of [the world's] activity.
(2.2.1) If it be argued that it is like milk or water, [we reply] that even in those cases [there is dependence].
(2.2.2) And because of the non-establishment of the distinction [between cause and effect], due to independence. (2.2.3)
And because [the effect] does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth;
if it is argued that it is like a person and a stone, even so,
it is not the case because the status of being the primary factor (aṅgin) is untenable.
Furthermore, [the doctrine is] inconsistent because, in the case of inference otherwise, there would be a lack of the capacity for knowledge;
even if it were accepted, there would be an absence of the object;
and because of contradiction, it is untenable.

Or, as with the "large" and the "long" [arising] from the "short" and the "circular," in neither case is there action; therefore, that [inherence] does not exist. Furthermore, because of the admission of inherence, and because of the resulting parity, there would be an infinite regress.
And because [the self] exists eternally;
and because there would be a reversal [of its nature] due to possessing form and so forth, as seen [in experience];
and because there are faults in both cases.
And because there is no grasping, there is absolute lack of dependence.
(BBs 2.2.16) Even if the collection [of causes] were due to both types of causes, that [collection] would not be attained.
(BBs 2.2.17) If it is argued that [the collection] is established through mutual conditionality, we say no, because it lacks the cause for the state of being a composite. (BBs 2.2.18)
Because the subsequent arises when the preceding has ceased;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction of the thesis or simultaneity.
There is no attainment of cessation through deliberation or non-deliberation, because there is no interruption.
Because there would be faults in either case;
because there is no distinction regarding space;
and because of recollection.
Not from the non-existent, because it is not observed;
and thus there would be the accomplishment of even those who are indifferent;
and non-existence [cannot be the cause], because of perception.
And because of dissimilarity, it is not like dreams and so forth;
there is no existence because of non-perception;
and because it is impossible in every way.
Because [the qualities] cannot exist in one [substratum];
and thus there would be incompleteness of the self;
nor is there non-contradiction even through succession, because of transformation and other [reasons].
And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both [causes] would be eternal, there is no distinction. (2,2.34) Because of the inconsistency of a Lord.
(2,2.35) And because of the impossibility of presiding over [the material cause]. (2,2.36)
If it is argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, no; because of enjoyment and so forth.
[The soul would have] either finitude or non-omniscience.
Because of the impossibility of its origination.
And there is no instrument for an agent;
or, if consciousness and so forth exist, there is no negation of that [agent];
and because of contradiction.
Space does not exist [as a substance], because it is not heard [in scripture] as such;
however, it does exist,
because figurative application is impossible and because of the scriptural word [for space].
And it might belong to one [of the two], like the word "Brahman" (BBs 2.3.4).
There would be an abandonment of the thesis because there is no distinction from the words (BBs 2.3.5). [This is known] from the words (BBs 2.3.6).
But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the world.
By this, air is explained.
But the non-existence of the existent is impossible, because it is not logically established.
Fire; for thus it says:
water; earth.
[The order of dissolution is established] from the context, the nature [of the things], and other words;
but from meditation on That alone, because of its characteristic mark, that [order] occurs;
however, the reverse order is also logically possible from this.

If it is argued that the intermediate state (*antarā-bhava*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the mind (*manas*) arise in succession because their respective marks appear in order, we say no, because there is no distinction [in the scriptural evidence].
(BBs 2.3.16) However, the designation [of the soul] as "moving" or "non-moving" would be figurative, based on its dependence upon those states, because it exists when they exist.
(BBs 2.3.17) The soul is not [produced], because of scripture and because of its eternity according to those [scriptures]. (BBs 2.3.18)
Therefore, [the soul] is a knower;
(2,3.19) because of its departure, its going, and its returning.
(2,3.20) And by its own self, it is [the agent] of the latter two. (2,3.21)
"If it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of the scriptural statement regarding its delight, we say no, because of the reference to the other [state];
and also because of the direct word and the measure;
and there is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood. (Brahma Sūtra 2.3.22–24)
If it is argued that [the soul's difference from the body] is due to a distinction in its state of residence, we say no, because [this is not accepted]; for [the soul] resides in the heart.
Or rather, [the soul's presence is] due to its quality, as in the case of the world.
Its separation is like that of fragrance; for scripture shows it thus.
Because it is taught separately [from the Self].
But that designation [of the Self] is due to its having those qualities as its essence, like the case of the "wise one" (prājña).
And because it persists as long as the existence of the body, there is no fault, since that [Self] is seen [to be distinct].
But [the Self] exists [prior to manifestation], because it is subject to manifestation, like masculinity and so forth.
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either its eternal perception or non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other.
[The Self is] an agent, because the scriptures have a purpose.
Because of appropriation and because of the teaching on abiding;
because of designation in action, provided there is no reversal of the instruction;
and because there is no restriction, as in the case of perception.
Because of the reversal of capacity;
because of the absence of meditative concentration;
and just as a carpenter [acts] in both ways.
But [the Self is] from another, because of the scriptural statement to that effect;
yet it depends on the effort performed by the individual, because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and so forth.
It is a part [of Brahman], because of various designations, and also because otherwise [it would not be possible]; for some record in their tradition its nature as a fisherman, a hunter, and so on.
From the wording of the mantra;
it is also recorded in the Smṛti.
But the Supreme is not like that, being like light and so forth.
And they record [this]:
"The permission and the exception [of certain actions] are due to the connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth;
and because there is no continuity [of the individual soul], there is no confusion [of karmic results]. (BBs 2.3.46–48)
And it is merely an appearance;
because there is no fixed rule regarding what is not seen;
and the same applies to intentions and so forth.
If it is argued that [the distinction] is due to a difference in location, we say no, because they are included within it.
Likewise, the vital breaths [are included].
Because a secondary sense is impossible, and because of their being heard [in scripture] prior to that.
Because speech is preceded by that [mind];
because the seven [organs] are distinguished by their mode of movement;
and because the hands and so forth exist when [the body] is stationary, it is not thus [with respect to them].
And [the self] is atomic;
it is also supreme.
The vital functions are not distinct from the air (vital breath), because they are taught separately.
But it is [an organ] like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and other such reasons (BBs 2.4.9).
And there is no fault because it is not an instrument; for thus he shows (BBs 2.4.10):
"It is designated as having five functions, like the mind" (BBs 2.4.11).

And [the soul] is atomic. But the light and so forth have Him as their presiding deity, because of the scriptural teaching concerning that, as in the case of the vital breath, and because of the word [of scripture], and because of His eternity.
Those [five] are the senses (indriya), because they are designated as such, except for the "best" one;
this is because of the scriptural mention of their distinction and because of their difference in nature.
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the triplication, according to the teaching.
Flesh and so forth belong to the earth, as does the other two [water and fire], according to their respective names.
But because of their specific distinction, they are so designated; such is the designation.
Upon entering into another body, it departs enveloped, as is established by the questions and the answers.
"But because [the subtle body] consists of three elements, because of their predominance,
because of the departure of the vital breath,
and because of the scriptural mention of fire and so forth— [if it be argued that the soul does not depart with the senses]— we say no, because these [scriptural statements] are figurative."
If it is argued that [the performers of sacrifices] do not go [to the moon] because they are not mentioned in the first [case], we say no; for it is logical that they are indeed those very ones.
If it is argued that this is so because they are not heard of [there], we say no; for those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* are understood [to be the ones].
Or rather, [their going] is figurative because they are not knowers of the Self; for the scripture shows it thus.
When the performed [karman] has reached its end, one who possesses residual karma (anuśaya) returns by the same way and not otherwise, as is seen from scripture and tradition.
If it is argued that this is not so because of [the mention of] conduct (caraṇa), we say no; for Kārṣṇājini holds that this is intended as an indication (upalakṣaṇa) of that [residual karma].
If it is argued that [the mention of conduct] would be purposeless, we say no; for it is dependent upon that [residual karma].
But Bādari [holds] that it is only good and evil deeds;
for there is also scriptural mention of those who perform undesirable acts and so forth.
However, after experiencing [the results] in the place of restraint (saṃyamana), there is ascent and descent for the others, as their course of travel is observed in scripture.
And they remember even up to seven [lives]. Even in that case, there is no contradiction because of the operation of that [meditative power].
"But because of the context of knowledge and action" (BBs 3.1.17);
"not in the third case, because it is not perceived as such" (BBs 3.1.18);
"and it is also recorded in common worldly usage" (BBs 3.1.19).
And because it is seen [in scripture].
(BBs 3.1.20) The third term [of the sūtra] includes that which arises from sorrow. (BBs 3.1.21) It attains its own inherent nature upon rebirth. (BBs 3.1.22)
Not after a long time, because of the distinction.

(BBs 3.1.23) Because of the expression [of the word] as before, even when presided over by another. (BBs 3.1.24) If it is argued that it is impure, no, because of the scriptural statement. (BBs 3.1.25)
Then, there is the union with the emitter of semen;
from the womb, the body [is produced].
For it says that creation occurs in the intermediate state (sandhya).
Some [hold that the world] has a creator, as well as sons and so forth;

however, it is merely an illusion because its true nature is entirely unmanifest. But through the meditation on the Supreme, [the Self] is concealed; for from that [concealment] come its bondage and its opposite.
Or rather, he [the soul] also [returns] due to its connection with the body;
for scripture indicates this, and those who know it declare so.
Its absence [from the heart] occurs in the channels and in the Self, according to scriptural testimony.
Therefore, awakening occurs from this [state].
But that [awakening] is indeed [immediate] because of action, recollection, word, and injunction. For one who is fainting, there is partial attainment [of death], by way of elimination.
The Supreme [Self] does not possess both characteristics even from the perspective of its location, for it is everywhere.
If it is argued that this is not so because of difference, we say no, because each [individual soul] is not described as being that [Supreme Self].
Moreover, some [scriptures] state it thus.
For that [consciousness] is indeed formless, because it is predominant;
and like light, it is not purposeless;
and he has said that it is "mere" [consciousness].
Furthermore, it is shown [in scripture] and also recorded in Smṛti.
For this very reason, there is a comparison with the reflection of the sun and so forth.
However, because [the Self] is not apprehended like water, it is not exactly like that.
[The soul] partakes of increase and decrease because it is included [within the body], because both [the individual and the universal] are thus consistent, and because such is seen [in scripture].
(3.2.20) For [the text] denies that the Self is limited to what has been previously described, and then declares more than that. (3.2.21) For [scripture] says that it is unmanifest. (3.2.22)
Moreover, [the Lord] is perceived through both direct perception and inference during the process of propitiation (saṃrādhana).
And just as light and so forth, there is no distinction [between the Lord and His powers], and this manifestation occurs in the act [of meditation] through practice.
Therefore, He is infinite; for such is the indicative mark (liṅga).
But [the relationship between Brahman and the world] is like that of a snake and its coils, because both designations apply;
or it is like light and its substratum, because of the nature of luminosity;
or it is as described previously.
And because of the prohibition [of other deities].
(BBs 3.2.29) Because of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and distinction from the perspective of another's doctrine.
(BBs 3.2.30) But on account of similarity. (BBs 3.2.31)
The [Self] exists for the sake of the intellect, like the feet;
because of the distinction of position, like light and so forth;
and because it is logical.
Likewise, because of the negation of others;
by this [sūtra], omnipresence [is established] from the words "extent" (āyāma) and so forth;
the fruit [proceeds] from Him, because it is logical.
And because it is so heard [in scripture].
(3.2.38) Jaimini [holds that] Dharma [is the object of the Vedas], for that very reason.
(3.2.39) But Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] the former [Brahman is the primary object], because of the designation of the cause. (3.2.40)
The knowledge derived from all Vedāntas is one and the same, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth.
If it be argued that it is not so because of differences [in ritual details], [we reply] that this applies even within a single Veda.

For the study of one's own Veda is likewise [uniform], and because of the qualification for the *Samācāra* (the rules of conduct), as in the case of the *Sava* sacrifice, there is a restriction to that [single Veda].
And it is shown [in scripture]:
"Because there is no difference in meaning, [the same rule applies] to the conclusion as to the rest of the injunction, when the case is identical.
(BBs 3.3.5) "If it be argued that there is a change [of state] because of the word, we say no, because there is no distinction. (BBs 3.3.6)
Or rather, it is not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of "the higher than the high" (parovarīyastva) and so forth.
If it is argued that it is so on account of the name, that has already been answered; moreover, that [name] also exists [elsewhere].
And because of its all-pervasiveness, [the designation of the heart] is appropriate.
These [attributes] are different because they are not common to all [the Upanishads].

(BBs 3.3.10) Bliss and the others belong to the Principal [Brahman]. (BBs 3.3.11) The state of having "pleasure as the head" and so forth is not attained [by Brahman], for increase and decrease occur only where there is difference. (BBs 3.3.12)
But the others [are to be meditated upon] because of the commonality of their meaning (BBs 3.3.13);
because there is no purpose for [further] meditation [on them individually] (BBs 3.3.14);
and because of the word "Self" (BBs 3.3.15).
The grasping of the Self [is taught] as in other cases, because of what follows (3.3.16).
If it is argued that it is so because of the logical connection (anvaya), it would be so because of the restrictive definition (3.3.17).
[The soul is] something not previously known, because of the description of its effects (kārya) (3.3.18).

It is the same because there is no distinction; (BBs 3.3.19) it is so because of the relationship even in other cases; (BBs 3.3.20) or rather, it is not so, because there is a distinction. (BBs 3.3.21)
And it shows [this];
for from this [text] there is both the gathering [of the fires] and their extension (BBs 3.3.22).
Also, because in the Puruṣavidyā the others are not mentioned (BBs 3.3.24).
Because there is a difference in meaning regarding piercing and so forth;
but in the case of departure, it is because the word for "taking up" is supplementary, as in the cases of the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the singing—so it has been stated.
Because there is nothing further to be crossed at the time of death, for thus say others.
By way of desire, because there is no contradiction between the two.

(BBs 3.3.28) The purposefulness of the destiny [of rebirth] exists in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction. (BBs 3.3.29) It is established that [the intermediate state] has arisen, because its characteristic object is perceived, as in the world. (BBs 3.3.30)
The abiding of those who hold office lasts as long as their office;
there is no fixed rule for all, as there is no contradiction with scripture and inference.

However, there is an inclusion of those who possess the cognition of the Imperishable, on account of the commonality and the presence of that state, as in the case of the *aupasada* sacrifice; this has been stated.
Because of this much being taught [in all the Upanishads].

(BBs 3.3.34) If it is argued that, as in the case of the "village of beings," there can be no difference from one's own self because it would otherwise be impossible, we say: No, for it is like the instruction. (BBs 3.3.35) There is a mutual exchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [the Self] as in the other cases. (BBs 3.3.36)
For those very [precepts] are "truth" and so forth;
desire and the rest [are excluded] elsewhere and there, except for the bases and so on;
there is no omission due to reverence.
Because it is so stated when [the sacrifice] has arrived;
there is no restriction regarding the determination of that [result], for it is seen separately, as its fruit is unobstructed,
just as it was declared in the case of the *pradāna*.
On account of the abundance of indicatory marks, that [meditation] is indeed stronger; even so,
the previous alternative may apply because of the context, as in the case of mental action,
and because of the extended application.
But it is knowledge alone [that is required], because of the definitive determination and because of scriptural vision;
and there is no sublation [of this view] because of the superior strength of direct Vedic statement (śruti) and the other means of proof.
On account of the "concomitance" (anubandha) and other factors, it is seen that there is a distinctness of cognitions, as has been stated.
Nor [is there non-existence] because of perception through generality, for there is no transition to another world, as in the case of death (BBs 3.3.49).
Furthermore, the word has that nature by virtue of another [scriptural passage], while its persistence is due to abundance (BBs 3.3.50).
[The soul is] one, because it exists in the body (BBs 3.3.51).
The distinction [of the rites] is due to their being contingent upon that [the person], and not because they are perceived [to be so], as in the case of the *upalabdhi* [meditations].
(BBs 3.3.52) But those [rites] connected with the limbs [of the sacrifice] do not belong to each specific branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda;
rather, there is no contradiction, just as in the case of the mantras and so forth. (BBs 3.3.53–54)
The greater excellence of the plenary [Brahman] is like that of a ritual; for thus scripture shows.
There is a plurality [of meditations] because of the difference in words and so forth.
There is an option [between them] because their fruits are not distinguished.
But the optional rites (kāmya) may be combined according to one's desire, or not, because of the absence of the aforementioned reason.
Regarding the subsidiaries (aṅga), there is the state of being dependent on their respective bases.
And because of the instruction [of the learned].
Because of their being combined;
because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities;
or rather, it is not so, because their coexistence is not stated in scripture.
And because it is seen [in scripture].
"Therefore, the human purpose [is attained] from the word," says Bādarāyaṇa.
"Because it is subordinate, it is a statement of human purpose, as in other cases," says Jaimini.
Because of the observation of [his] conduct;
because of the hearing of that [from him];
because of [his] taking hold [of the disciple].
Because [the scripture] prescribes [the rites] for one who possesses that [knowledge];
because of the restrictive rule;
and because of the additional instruction, Bādarāyaṇa holds this view, for such is seen in the scriptures.
But the vision is equal;
it is not universal.
Its distribution is like that of a hundred [pieces of gold].
[The qualification applies] to one who possesses the mere study [of the Veda];
not so, because there is no distinction [stated];
or rather, it is a permission for the sake of praise.
And some [hold that there is no fault] by acting according to one's own will;
[there is also no fault] in the suppression [of desire];
and because the word [is used] with respect to those whose semen is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas).

Jaimini holds that there is no injunction [regarding the wearing of the staff], for he rejects it as being mere grasping; Bādarāyaṇa, however, maintains that it is to be performed because of the scriptural statement of its equality,
or rather, it is an injunction like the wearing [of the sacred thread].

If it is argued that [the passages] are merely for the purpose of praise because they are based on [already known matters], we say no, because they convey something not previously established (apūrvatva),
and because they consist of words denoting existence (bhāva).
If it is argued that they have the purpose of mere narrative wandering (pāriplava), we say no, because they are specified [as having a specific purpose].
And likewise, because of the connection within a single sentence;
and for this very reason, there is no dependence on firewood and the like;
and there is dependence on everything, because of the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse.
Nevertheless, one should be endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth; for since those are enjoined as auxiliary parts of that [knowledge], they too must necessarily be practiced.

(BBs 3.4.27) And there is no permission for all [actions] except in the case of life-threatening danger, because that is seen [in scripture]. (BBs 3.4.28) And because there is no contradiction. (BBs 3.4.29)
Moreover, it is recorded in Smṛti:
"And for this reason, there is a scriptural prohibition against acting according to one's own will;
and because they are enjoined, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must also be performed."
And by way of cooperation;
in every respect, those very [elements] [are established] because of their dual characteristics;
and he demonstrates non-overpowering.
Moreover, it is seen even in the interval;
it is also remembered;
and there is the favoring of specific distinctions.
But the other [state] is superior to this, both because of a scriptural mark and because of a logical sign (liṅga).
But for one who has become that [Brahman], there is no becoming otherwise, according to Jaimini as well, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of those characteristics.
Nor does the status of one holding an office [prevent falling], because of the inference of falling and because of the impossibility of that [status] remaining.
Some say that even when preceded by the prefix *upa*, [the term] denotes a state (*bhāva*), as in the case of *aśana*; this has been stated [in the Sūtra].
(BBs 3.4.42) But outside [of Vedic ritual], it is both ways, according to Smṛti and established usage.
(BBs 3.4.43) Ātreya says [that the fruit belongs to the sacrificer] because the scripture declares the fruit for the master (*svāmin*). (BBs 3.4.44)
"Regarding the office of the officiating priest (*ārṭvijya*), Auḍulomi [says] that it is for this purpose that [the seeker] is hired.
(BBs 3.4.45) "It is an injunction for another auxiliary, as an alternative; it belongs to one who possesses [the previous qualification], like the beginning of an injunction.
(BBs 3.4.46) "But because of the state of being complete, the conclusion is made with the householder. (BBs 3.4.47)
Because there is instruction for others as well, just as for the practice of silence;
because [the fruit] follows from not manifesting [the knowledge];
and because we observe that the fruit belongs to this life when there is no obstruction of what has been commenced.
Thus, there is no restriction regarding the fruits of liberation because that state is determined; because that state is determined. There is a return [to this world] because of repeated instruction;
and because of an inferential mark.
"But they approach [the Self] as 'Self' and cause others to grasp it as such; for it is not in a symbol, for He is not that.
The vision of Brahman [is applied to the symbol] because of its excellence."
And the meditations on the sun and so forth are [to be performed] upon the limbs [of the sacrifice], because that is appropriate;
[the meditation is] seated, because it is possible [only thus];
and because of the mention of "meditation" (dhyāna).
And with reference to immovability;
and they remember it;
wherever there is one-pointedness, there [it exists] without distinction.
For even there, [the result of action] is seen until death (ā-prayāṇāt).
Upon the attainment of that [knowledge], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof.
For the other [merit] as well, there is likewise non-clinging; but at the falling away [of the body], [there is experience].
But the former [works] alone have their effects not yet begun, for that is the limit [of their influence].
However, the Agnihotra and other such rites are for the sake of that very effect [liberation], because it is so seen in scripture.
For this reason, according to some, there is another [type of work] belonging to both.
"For [the soul departs] by means of knowledge alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).
But others, having exhausted [their karma] through experience, then attain [Brahman].
Speech merges into the mind, because of both scriptural statement and logical reasoning. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6)
For this very reason, [the soul] follows after all [the senses]; that mind [follows] the vital breath, according to the subsequent [scriptural passage];
and that [vital breath] follows the presiding deity (the individual soul), because of its approaching that [deity] and other reasons.
[The soul's departure] is with respect to all beings, because that is what is heard [in scripture];
for [the scriptures] show it to be not [limited] to one [class of beings].
And [this departure] is common [to all] until the beginning of the path, and immortality [is attained] without having burned away [all karmic residues].
"Even then [the subtle body persists], because the state of transmigratory existence is designated until that [liberation];
it is subtle, both by its own nature and because it is perceived as such;
therefore, it cannot be destroyed."
And from this very reasoning follows the intermediate state (*ūṣman*).
If it is argued that [the soul] does not go forth because of a prohibition, we say no; for according to some, it is clearly stated to depart from the body.
And it is also recorded in tradition (*smṛti*).
Regarding those [fires], others [say] as follows:
"Because of the scriptural statement, there is no division" (BBs 4.2.14).

"Then there is the blazing of the flame at the top of the heart; the door is illuminated by that, due to the power of knowledge and because of the application of the recollection of the path which is the remainder of that [knowledge]" (BBs 4.2.15–16).
[The soul] follows the rays;
if it is argued that this does not occur at night, we say no, because the connection [between the soul and the rays] persists as long as the body exists, and scripture also demonstrates this.
Therefore, [the soul goes to Brahman] even during the southern course of the sun.
These two [paths] are recorded in the Smṛti for yogins, and they are indeed based on the Smṛti;
(BBs 4.2.20) because that [attainment] is well-known through the path beginning with light (arcis);
(BBs 4.3.1) [the soul goes] from the year to the wind, on account of both the lack of distinction and the presence of distinction. (BBs 4.3.2)
Varuṇa [is reached] after the lightning, because of their connection;
the *ātivāhika* [guides] [are implied] because of the indicative mark thereof;
and from there, [the soul goes] by means of the lightning alone, because of the scriptural statement to that effect.
Bādari [holds that the soul goes] to the effected [Brahman], because the movement [of the soul] is thus logically established (4.3.6),
and because [the soul] is specified [as such] (4.3.7).
But the designation of that [effected Brahman] is due to its proximity [to the unqualified Brahman] (4.3.8).
Because of the statement that [the soul] departs together with its presiding deity at the end of its task;
because of the Smṛti;
and because Jaimini holds that it goes to the highest [Brahman], since that is the primary meaning.
And because of the scriptural vision [of the soul departing with the vital functions];
and there is no intention regarding the effect [the body].
Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the Lord] leads those who do not have the *pratīka* as their support, because there would be faults in both cases, and because of the person's resolve (*tatkratu*).
And he shows the distinction:
"The manifestation [of the self] occurs by its own nature, because of the scriptural statement";
"It is liberated, because it is so asserted."
The Self [is the subject], because of the context;
because it is seen as non-differentiated;
Jaimini [holds that the soul attains] the state of Brahman, on account of the introductory statements and so forth.
"Because he consists of that [mind] alone, [the soul exists] as mere consciousness; thus says Auḍulomi.
"Even so, because of the introductory statement and because of its prior existence, there is no contradiction; thus says Bādarāyaṇa.
"Because of that scriptural statement, [he creates] from intention alone."
For this very reason, there is no other presiding deity.
Bādari says it is non-existence, for he speaks thus; Jaimini says it is existence, because of the meditation on the alternative.
Therefore, Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the intermediate state] is of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice;
for when there is no body, it is logical that it is like the twilight [state],
and when there is a body, it is like the waking state.
The entry [of the soul] is like that of a lamp; for thus the scripture shows (BBs 4.4.15).
For it is made manifest with reference to either deep sleep or union [with Brahman] (BBs 4.4.16).
[The Lord's power] is excluded from the activity of the world, because of the context and because of His non-proximity [to that activity] (BBs 4.4.17).
If it is argued that [the Lord] is perceived because of direct instruction, we say no; for what is stated refers to those situated within the spheres of authority.
And He does not abide in the realm of transformation, for thus He declares His state of being.
Furthermore, both perception and inference demonstrate this.
And because there is a mark indicating equality in respect to enjoyment alone;
"No return, on account of the scriptural statement; no return, on account of the scriptural statement."
